{
"title": "A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12",
"authors": "Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris",
"field_subfield": "Materials Science / Computational Chemistry",
"type_of_paper": "Methodology / Computational Study",
"executive_summary": "This study addresses the lack of consensus regarding the ground state configuration of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a critical solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries. The authors present a novel workflow to systematically identify energetically favorable configurations by first eliminating physically impossible structures with overlapping lithium atoms using a 1.7 Å cutoff. Symmetry-equivalent duplicates are then removed using local sensitive hashing, reducing the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10^8 to ~2 × 10^6 unique structures. A machine learning-based multiple linear regression model, trained on Density Functional Theory (DFT) data, is used to energetically order the remaining structures. The results indicate that the vast majority of previously reported structures in the literature violate the minimal Li-Li distance constraint, suggesting they are not physically feasible. The study identifies four low-energy structures with a 24d:96h occupancy ratio of 8:48, all within 0.026 eV of the global minimum. The authors provide a freely accessible database of these generated structures to improve reproducibility in future research. The work highlights that entropic contributions and geometry relaxation were not fully included in the final energetic ordering, representing a limitation of the current approach.",

summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the lack of consensus regarding the ground state configuration of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a critical solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries. The authors present a novel workflow to systematically identify energetically favorable configurations by first eliminating physically impossible structures with overlapping lithium atoms using a 1.7 Å cutoff. Symmetry-equivalent duplicates are then removed using local sensitive hashing, reducing the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10^8 to ~2 × 10^6 unique structures. A machine learning-based multiple linear regression model, trained on Density Functional Theory (DFT) data, is used to energetically order the remaining structures. The results indicate that the vast majority of previously reported structures in the literature violate the minimal Li-Li distance constraint, suggesting they are not physically feasible. The study identifies four low-energy structures with a 24d:96h occupancy ratio of 8:48, all within 0.026 eV of the global minimum. The authors provide a freely accessible database of these generated structures to improve reproducibility in future research. The work highlights that entropic contributions and geometry relaxation were not fully included in the final energetic ordering, representing a limitation of the current approach.

The 24d:96h occupancy ratio of 8:48 is energetically preferred for c-LLZO.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the lack of consensus regarding the ground state configuration of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a critical solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries. The authors present a novel workflow to systematically identify energetically favorable configurations by first eliminating physically impossible structures with overlapping lithium atoms using a 1.7 Å cutoff. Symmetry-equivalent duplicates are then removed using local sensitive hashing, reducing the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10^8 to ~2 × 10^6 unique structures. A machine learning-based multiple linear regression model, trained on Density Functional Theory (DFT) data, is used to energetically order the remaining structures. The results indicate that the vast majority of previously reported structures in the literature violate the minimal Li-Li distance constraint, suggesting they are not physically feasible. The study identifies four low-energy structures with a 24d:96h occupancy ratio of 8:48, all within 0.026 eV of the global minimum. The authors provide a freely accessible database of these generated structures to improve reproducibility in future research. The work highlights that entropic contributions and geometry relaxation were not fully included in the final energetic ordering, representing a limitation of the current approach.

Research Context
Solid electrolytes offer higher energy density and safety. c-LLZO has the best interfacial stability against metallic Li. There is no consensus of c-LLZO's Li occupancy. Computational studies rely on an initial low-energy structure. Without knowing if structures are close to the ground state, properties may not be well described.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to find and rank all possible Li site occupancies. We intend to produce all possible structures of a c-LLZO unit cell. We hope to elicit whether some structural properties are indicative of energy. We hypothesize that a large portion of previously reported structures may not be feasible. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO). c-LLZO has a Hermann-Maguin space group of Ia 3d. Li atoms partially occupy the 24d and 96h sites. The 24d site is tetrahedral and the 96h site occurs at a tetrahedral/octahedral interface. We begin by eliminating structures that involve overlapping Li atoms. We impose a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å. This constraint limits the physically possible 24d :96h ratios. A maximum of 48 out of 96h sites can be occupied at any one time. Each of the 24d occupation eliminates 4 out of 96h sites. We initially generate all possible 24d permutations for a given 24d occupancy. We populate the remaining 96h sites such that no two nearest neighbours are occupied simultaneously. The number of structures for each 24d :96h ratio, for one unit cell, are given in Table 1. We use the crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al. 19 as our framework. This method will generate all possible structures, approximately 2.3 × 10 8. We construct the upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice for each structure. We use local sensitive hashing (LSH) to perform fast approximate similarity searches. The use of LSH optimises the pairwise comparison from scaling at O(N 2 ) to O(N ). This symmetry comparison method allows us to perform symmetry checks on over 100 million structures. Employing this technique we find that only approximately 1% of our structures are symmetrically unique. Having reduced the configuration space to around 2 × 10 6 structures we can energetically order our structures. We perform DFT calculations on small subsets of the total number of structures. The first subset was the 200 energetically lowest structures according to the COMPASSIII forcefield. The second subset was a random selection of approximately 1000 structures across the entire configuration space. In total 1235 single point DFT calculations were performed. All DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code. We use the PBE GGA exchange correlation functional. We use a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV. The structures were represented by a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions. The data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio.

Procedures And Architectures
We assume the base LaZrO structure remains relatively unchanged with each configuration. An expression of all types of Li interactions would be a sufficient descriptor for predicting the energies. The DFT energies were paired with a numerical representation of the structure and fit using a multiple linear regression model (MLR). We found through applying this model to our test set a correlation of 0.9996. All structures are found to occur within a range of 5.8 eV of our lowest energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. The 19 th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground state structures. There are four structures, all 8:48, within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest energy structure. The four lowest energy have very similar atomic coordinates. We perform geometry optimisation calculations on the final four structures. We note that our energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. We assume a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. We have tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. A large-scale energy prediction of the geometry optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication. We use the COMPASSIII forcefield when applied to only the Li-sublattice. It was able to order the 13:43 with a correlation coefficient of 0.991. Figure S3 shows that COMPASSIII predicts a more pronounced separation of energies. We use the atomic simulation environment (ASE) python package's symmetry equivalence check. We assigned the new space groups for all 2 × 10 6 symmetry unique structures. The most symmetric ratio appears to be 8:48 followed by 12:44 and finally 10:46. We tested including the symmetry of the structure in our MLR model but found it made a negligible difference. We perform 20 geometry optimisation calculations. We use the Broyder-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) method. The 96h to 24d transition was only recorded once and yielded our lowest overall energy structure. The 96h to 24d transition meant that the ratio of the structure changed from 9:47 to 10:46. In figure S7a there is a negative correlation between the mean distance moved of all Li atoms and increasing energy. These results indicate that from the structures assessed movement from original sites is preferable to attain lower energies.

Key Results
We eliminate structures that involve overlapping Li atoms based on nearest neighbour counts. We further reduce the configuration space by eliminating symmetry images from all remaining structures. This is followed up with a machine learning-based energetic ordering of all remaining structures. We find that only approximately 1% of our structures are symmetrically unique. The correlation of the MLR model on the test set is 0.9996. All structures are found to occur within a range of 5.8 eV of our lowest energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. The 19 th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground state structures. There are four structures, all 8:48, within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest energy structure. The four lowest energy have very similar atomic coordinates. The energy gap between them narrows further after geometry optimisation. The 96h to 24d transition yielded our lowest overall energy structure. The 96h to 24d transition meant that the ratio of the structure changed from 9:47 to 10:46. The lowest overall energy structure is 0.58 eV lower in energy than the geometry optimised lowest energy single point structure. There is a negative correlation between the mean distance moved of all Li atoms and increasing energy. A large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature are predicting or working with structures that are not reflective of a real system.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
We determine that a large portion of previously reported structures may not be feasible or stable. The method developed here could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. We provide all structures generated in a freely accessible database. We hope to improve accuracy and reproducibility in future c-LLZO research. The energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. We assume a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. These results indicate that from the structures assessed movement from original sites is preferable to attain lower energies. The study highlights that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature are predicting or working with structures that are not reflective of a real system.

Contradictions And Limitations
We neglect to include the 48g site that occurs between the 96h sites as it is not reported in most refinements we find. Our energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. We assume a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. A large-scale energy prediction of the geometry optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication. We use the COMPASSIII forcefield when applied to only the Li-sublattice. COMPASSIII predicts a more pronounced separation of energies depending on the 24d :96h ratio than is predicted by ONETEP. This issue was considered too large to surmount in this paper. We tested including the symmetry of the structure in our MLR model but found it made a negligible difference. The 96h to 24d transition was only recorded once and yielded our lowest overall energy structure. The 96h to 24d transition meant that the ratio of the structure changed from 9:47 to 10:46.

Claims
A large portion of previously reported c-LLZO structures are physically infeasible due to overlapping Li atoms. We begin by eliminating structures that involve overlapping Li atoms. We impose a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å. A large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature are predicting or working with structures that are not reflective of a real system. Experimental assignments used neutron diffraction or x-ray diffraction. We provide all structures generated in a freely accessible database. We hope to improve accuracy and reproducibility in future c-LLZO research.
The 24d:96h occupancy ratio of 8:48 is energetically preferred for c-LLZO. 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. The average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy. There are four structures, all 8:48, within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest energy structure. The 96h to 24d transition yielded our lowest overall energy structure. The 96h to 24d transition meant that the ratio of the structure changed from 9:47 to 10:46. The method developed here could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Data And Code Availability
We provide all structures generated in a freely accessible database. The structures produced in this work are be published alongside our results. Both scripts are provided with our database in SI section.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
We validated this method for both 13:43 and 12:44 ratios. We use the atomic simulation environment (ASE) python package's symmetry equivalence check. In both cases the same number of structures were produced using either method. We tested including the symmetry of the structure in our MLR model but found it made a negligible difference. We have tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. None of these site changes correlated significantly with the geometry optimised energy.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1b shows the c-LLZO structure with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites. Figure 1c shows the lack of consensus of c-LLZO's Li occupancy. Figure 2b shows that 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. Figure 3 shows the workflow we employ to find our 4 final structures from given occupancies. Table 1 gives the number of structures for each 24d :96h ratio, for one unit cell. Table S1 summarizes all experimental papers that explicitly report the site occupancies. Table S2 summarizes all theoretical studies that explicitly report their 24d :96h ratio.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a workflow to identify viable crystal structures with partially occupied sites. 2. The strongest evidence is that 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. 3. The future path is to extend the method to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.
